rules.title: -able versus -ible endings
rules.short_explanation: Some adjectives end in -able and others in -ible, and there is no simple rule, so these words are often best learned individually, like available and possible.
rules.tts_text: Some words end in able, others end in ible.
rules.mnemonic: Able is common; ible likes to hide in short roots.

rules.title: Accept or except
rules.short_explanation: Accept means to agree to take something. Except means not including.
rules.tts_text: Listen and choose the correct form.
rules.mnemonic: Accept an offer; except one item.

rules.title: Advice or advise
rules.short_explanation: Advice is a noun for a suggestion. Advise is a verb meaning to give a suggestion.
rules.tts_text: Listen and choose the correct form.
rules.mnemonic: Advice is a thing; advise is an action.

rules.title: Affect vs effect
rules.short_explanation: Affect is usually a verb meaning to influence something. Effect is usually a noun meaning the result.
rules.tts_text: Affect versus effect
rules.mnemonic: Affect = Action, Effect = End result.

rules.title: Common irregular past verbs
rules.short_explanation: Many common verbs change spelling in the past. Buy becomes bought, teach becomes taught, and think becomes thought.
rules.tts_text: Listen and choose the correct form.
rules.mnemonic: Bought, brought and thought share ought.

rules.title: Common irregular plurals
rules.short_explanation: Some plural nouns do not use -s or -es. Child becomes children, mouse becomes mice and person becomes people.
rules.tts_text: Listen and choose the correct form.
rules.mnemonic: Child becomes children; mouse becomes mice.

rules.title: Comparatives with -er and -est
rules.short_explanation: Short adjectives often add -er or -est. Double a final consonant after a short vowel, change final y to i, or drop a final e.
rules.tts_text: Listen and choose the correct form.
rules.mnemonic: Big doubles; happy changes y; nice drops e.

rules.title: Double consonants
rules.short_explanation: Some common words need doubled letters. Learn the whole visual pattern instead of relying only on sound.
rules.tts_text: Double consonants
rules.mnemonic: Tomorrow has a double r; useful has one l.

rules.title: Doubling before -ing and -ed
rules.short_explanation: Short verbs that end in one vowel and one consonant often double the final consonant before -ing or -ed, as in plan becoming planning.
rules.tts_text: Double the final consonant before ing or ed.
rules.mnemonic: One vowel, one consonant, double before you go on.

rules.title: Dropping the silent e
rules.short_explanation: When a verb ends in a silent e, you usually drop the e before adding -ing or -ed. For example, make becomes making.
rules.tts_text: Drop the silent e before ing or ed.
rules.mnemonic: The silent e steps aside to let -ing and -ed in.

rules.title: Forming adverbs with -ly
rules.short_explanation: Most adverbs are formed by adding -ly to an adjective, but adjectives ending in y usually change to i before -ly, as in happy becoming happily.
rules.tts_text: Change y to i before adding ly.
rules.mnemonic: Happy waves goodbye to y and says hi to ily.

rules.title: Irregular past: go / went
rules.short_explanation: Go does not take -ed in the past tense. Its past form is the irregular word went.
rules.tts_text: Irregular past of go
rules.mnemonic: Go, went, gone — learn the whole set together.

rules.title: Its vs it's
rules.short_explanation: Its (no apostrophe) shows that something belongs to it. It's is short for it is or it has.
rules.tts_text: Its versus it is
rules.mnemonic: If you can say "it is", use it's.

rules.title: Keep e after soft c and g
rules.short_explanation: Keep e after soft c or g before a suffix beginning with a or o. Notice becomes noticeable, and courage becomes courageous.
rules.tts_text: Listen and choose the correct form.
rules.mnemonic: Keep e so c and g stay soft.

rules.title: Lose vs loose
rules.short_explanation: Lose is a verb meaning to not have something anymore. Loose is an adjective meaning not tight.
rules.tts_text: Lose versus loose
rules.mnemonic: One O in lose, like losing one letter.

rules.title: Nouns ending in -ance or -ence
rules.short_explanation: Some nouns end in -ance, like appearance. Others end in -ence, like difference and independence.
rules.tts_text: Listen and choose the correct form.
rules.mnemonic: Appearance takes ance; difference takes ence.

rules.title: Nouns ending in -tion or -sion
rules.short_explanation: Some nouns end in -tion, like information. Others end in -sion, like decision and discussion. Learn the ending with each word.
rules.tts_text: Listen and choose the correct form.
rules.mnemonic: Information takes tion; decision takes sion.

rules.title: Plural nouns with -es
rules.short_explanation: Add -es to most nouns ending in s, x, z, ch or sh. Box becomes boxes.
rules.tts_text: Listen and choose the correct form.
rules.mnemonic: A hissing ending needs an extra e.

rules.title: Plural nouns with -ves
rules.short_explanation: Some nouns ending in f or fe change that ending to -ves in the plural. Knife becomes knives.
rules.tts_text: Listen and choose the correct form.
rules.mnemonic: A knife loses fe and gains ves.

rules.title: Plural: y becomes ies
rules.short_explanation: When a noun ends in a consonant plus y, change y to i and add es to form the plural.
rules.tts_text: Plural y to ies
rules.mnemonic: Company to companies; one lonely y turns into two i's.

rules.title: Practice or practise
rules.short_explanation: In British English, practice is a noun. Practise is a verb.
rules.tts_text: Listen and choose the correct form.
rules.mnemonic: Practise with s is something you do.

rules.title: Principal or principle
rules.short_explanation: Principal means main or a head teacher. Principle is a basic belief or rule.
rules.tts_text: Listen and choose the correct form.
rules.mnemonic: Principal is main; principle is a rule.

rules.title: Quiet or quite
rules.short_explanation: Quiet means making little noise. Quite means fairly or rather.
rules.tts_text: Listen and choose the correct form.
rules.mnemonic: Quiet sounds soft; quite means fairly.

rules.title: Silent letters
rules.short_explanation: Some English words contain letters that are written but not pronounced. Learning these silent letters helps you spell tricky words correctly.
rules.tts_text: Some letters in English words are silent.
rules.mnemonic: The k in knife is silent, just like the w in write.

rules.title: Stationary or stationery
rules.short_explanation: Stationary means not moving. Stationery means paper and writing supplies.
rules.tts_text: Listen and choose the correct form.
rules.mnemonic: Stationery has e for envelopes.

rules.title: The suffix -ful has one L
rules.short_explanation: The suffix -ful always has a single l, as in useful and careful, even though the word full has two.
rules.tts_text: The suffix ful has only one l.
rules.mnemonic: Ful is never full of extra Ls.

rules.title: Then or than
rules.short_explanation: Then refers to time or the next step. Than is used when comparing things.
rules.tts_text: Listen and choose the correct form.
rules.mnemonic: Then is time; than compares.

rules.title: There vs their vs they're
rules.short_explanation: There points to a place or starts a sentence (there is). Their shows that something belongs to them. They're is short for they are.
rules.tts_text: There, their, and they are
rules.mnemonic: Their has "heir" in it: it belongs to someone.

rules.title: To, too or two
rules.short_explanation: To shows direction or comes before a verb. Too means also or excessively; two means the number 2.
rules.tts_text: Listen and choose the correct form.
rules.mnemonic: Two is a number; too is extra.

rules.title: Vowel order: i and e
rules.short_explanation: The order of i and e changes the spelling of a word. After c, most words use ei.
rules.tts_text: Vowel order i and e
rules.mnemonic: After c, use ei: receive.

rules.title: Weather or whether
rules.short_explanation: Weather is the condition outside. Whether introduces a question or a choice.
rules.tts_text: Listen and choose the correct form.
rules.mnemonic: Weather is outside; whether is a choice.

rules.title: Were, where or wear
rules.short_explanation: Were is a past form of be. Where asks about a place; wear means to have clothes on.
rules.tts_text: Listen and choose the correct form.
rules.mnemonic: Where is a place; wear is clothes.

rules.title: Your vs you're
rules.short_explanation: Your shows that something belongs to you. You're is short for you are.
rules.tts_text: Your versus you are
rules.mnemonic: If you can say "you are", use you're.

rules.title: A or an: the sound decides
rules.short_explanation: Use a before a consonant SOUND and an before a vowel SOUND. Listen to the first sound of the next word, not its first letter: an hour (the h is silent), a university (it starts with the sound "yoo").
rules.tts_text: Use a before a consonant sound and an before a vowel sound.
rules.mnemonic: Say the next word aloud. Does it start with a vowel sound? Then an.

rules.title: A or the: new or already known?
rules.short_explanation: Use a / an when you mention something for the first time or mean any one of its kind. Use the when the listener already knows which one: it was mentioned before, it is clear from the situation, or there is only one.
rules.tts_text: Use a for something new, and the for something already known.
rules.mnemonic: A: any one, new. The: that one, we both know it.

rules.title: The with one-of-a-kind things, superlatives and ordinals
rules.short_explanation: Use the when there is only one: the sun, the moon, the Internet. Use the with superlatives (the best, the most beautiful), with ordinals (the first, the second) and with the only / the same / the next / the last.
rules.tts_text: Use the with things that are unique, superlatives and ordinal numbers.
rules.mnemonic: Only one? The. Best, first, last, only? The.

rules.title: No article for things in general
rules.short_explanation: When you talk about a whole group or an idea in general, use no article with plural and uncountable nouns: I love music. Cats are independent. Life is not easy. Use the only when you mean something specific: The music at the party was too loud.
rules.tts_text: Use no article for plural and uncountable nouns when you mean them in general.
rules.mnemonic: In general: nothing. Specific: the.

rules.title: No article: names, meals, languages, sports
rules.short_explanation: Use no article with names of people, most cities and countries, languages, sports and the meals: Paris, Canada, French, football, breakfast. If you add an adjective to a meal, you need a: We had a wonderful lunch.
rules.tts_text: No article with names, languages, sports and meals.
rules.mnemonic: Names, languages, games and meals walk alone.

rules.title: The with rivers, seas, mountain ranges and plural countries
rules.short_explanation: Use the with oceans, seas, rivers and mountain ranges (the Atlantic, the Thames, the Alps), with plural names (the Netherlands, the United States) and with countries that have words like Kingdom, Republic or States in the name. Most single countries, cities, lakes and single mountains take no article: Japan, Lake Geneva, Mount Everest.
rules.tts_text: Use the with oceans, rivers, mountain ranges and plural country names.
rules.mnemonic: Water and groups take the. Single places walk alone.

rules.title: Routine places and transport: go to school, by bus
rules.short_explanation: Some places and times are used for their normal purpose and take no article: go to school (as a pupil), go to work, be at home, go to bed, at night, by bus, by train. If you mean the building or one particular thing, use the: I am going to the school to speak to the teacher.
rules.tts_text: No article with routine places and with by plus transport.
rules.mnemonic: Normal use: no article. A particular building: the.

rules.title: A / an with jobs, per, and quantity words
rules.short_explanation: Use a / an with a job when you say what someone is: She is a teacher. Use a / an to mean per: twice a week, ten pounds an hour. Quantity expressions also take a: a few, a little, a lot of, half an hour, such a, what a. Few and little without a mean "not enough".
rules.tts_text: Use a or an with jobs, with per, and in a few, a little, such a, what a.
rules.mnemonic: A job, a week, a few, a little: the little word a is needed.
